summary: Describes login referrals for IMAP4. When users are moved between servers, a server can redirect a client to the new home server so connecting still works. This helps sites with many users and many IMAP servers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2221 lets an IMAP4 server tell a client to connect to another server for a user's mailboxes. A direct client connection can avoid making the first server relay all mailbox data.

subtitle: How an IMAP4 server can direct a client to the server holding a user's mailboxes.

tldr.problem: Users may move between IMAP4 servers, and clients need a way to find the server that now holds their personal mailboxes.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises LOGIN-REFERRALS and returns a referral response containing an IMAP URL for another server.
tldr.outcome: The client can connect directly to the referred server; it must not follow more than 10 referral levels without consulting the user.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 2221's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC specifies the IMAP4 LOGIN-REFERRALS extension.

sections.title: Why an IMAP Client May Be Referred
sections.content:
Large services may need to move users from one IMAP4 server to another because of hardware failures or organizational changes. A login referral lets the client connect to the user's new home server.

This can use less bandwidth than a proxy arrangement in which the original server contacts the remote server and relays data back to the client. It also avoids requiring the original server to impersonate the client when authenticating to the remote server.
sections.plainLanguage: If a user's mailbox moves, the first server can give the client the new server's address. The client then connects to that server directly.

sections.title: Recognizing and Following Referrals
sections.content:
An IMAP4 server that supports this extension must include LOGIN-REFERRALS in its CAPABILITY response. A referral uses a response code containing a valid IMAP server URL and can appear during login or in a connection-startup response.

A referral may be returned when a server does not contain the user's mailboxes, or when it is not accepting connections. Clients must not follow more than 10 referral levels without consulting the user, and a server should avoid referring clients to a server that will refer them again.
sections.plainLanguage: The server identifies the referral feature and returns an IMAP address for another server. The client follows the address, with a limit on chains of referrals.

sections.title: What the Referral Response Means
sections.content:
A tagged NO referral means that the server has no mailboxes accessible to the user. A tagged OK referral means the user's personal mailboxes are elsewhere, though the server may still provide public mailboxes the user can read.

The client cannot infer from a home-server referral whether the move is permanent or temporary. A server must not issue a login referral when authentication for that user fails, so it does not reveal account information to an unauthorized user.
sections.plainLanguage: The response tells the client whether personal mailboxes are elsewhere and whether public mailboxes remain available. It does not say whether the move is permanent.
